lesson.title: Four Algorithms, One Handshake
lesson.summary: A cipher suite is the specific combination of key exchange, authentication, encryption, and integrity algorithms that a client and server agree to use for a TLS session, and picking a weak one can undermine an otherwise well designed connection.
lesson.body:
When two systems set up a TLS connection, they don't just decide to use encryption in general. They negotiate a very particular list of cryptographic building blocks, and that list is called a cipher suite. A cipher suite names four separate jobs and, for each one, which specific algorithm will handle that job for the lifetime of the session: how the two sides will agree on a shared secret (key exchange), how each side will prove its identity (authentication), how the actual data will be scrambled (bulk encryption), and how each side will detect if a message was tampered with in transit (message authentication).

A typical cipher suite name makes this concrete. Something like TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 is really four decisions packed into one label: ECDHE handles key exchange (elliptic curve Diffie Hellman with ephemeral keys, meaning a fresh secret is generated for this session and discarded afterward), RSA handles authentication (the server proves who it is using its RSA key pair and certificate), AES_128_GCM handles bulk encryption of the actual traffic, and SHA256 supports the message integrity portion of the exchange. This connects directly to symmetric encryption: once the key exchange step produces a shared secret, that secret is used to key a fast symmetric cipher like AES, because symmetric algorithms are far more efficient than public key algorithms for encrypting large volumes of data.

Why negotiate at all instead of hardcoding one combination everywhere? Because clients and servers vary in age and capability, and cryptography evolves as weaknesses are found in older algorithms. During the TLS handshake, the client sends a list of cipher suites it supports, ordered by preference, and the server picks one from that list that it also supports. This flexibility is also the reason cipher suite choice matters so much for security: a suite is only as strong as its weakest component. If a server still accepts a cipher suite with an outdated encryption algorithm, an attacker who can influence the negotiation may try to steer the connection toward that weaker option, a category of attack often called a downgrade attack. This is why modern practice leans toward disabling old cipher suites entirely on both client and server, rather than trusting that the strongest available option will always be the one chosen.

It's worth being precise about what a cipher suite is not. It is not the TLS protocol itself, TLS is the overall handshake and record protocol that establishes and protects the connection. The cipher suite is the specific set of algorithmic choices made within that handshake for a given session. Two connections both using TLS can end up with completely different cipher suites depending on what each side supports and prefers, which is why checking exactly which cipher suites a server is willing to negotiate is a standard part of any security review.
